title: AI Doctors Share Fake Health Tips on Social Media
paragraphs: Social media has long been a source of unreliable health advice, but experts warn that the problem is now being made worse by AI-generated "doctors" who look and sound convincing but share false information.

In July 2026, Hallam, a digital marketing agency in the UK, published research based on an analysis of 1,198 TikTok videos. It found that 40% of the most-viewed health videos contained AI-generated content. When the researchers searched for "health tips," the figure rose to 84%. The most popular AI-generated videos had an average of 2.5 million views each.

Many of these videos combine reasonable-sounding wellness advice with well-known myths. Some of the false claims included the idea that microwaving food in plastic causes cancer and that a spoonful of Coca-Cola mixed with onion can relieve pain. Other videos claimed that turmeric lowers high blood sugar or that raw cacao and beetroot can "unclog your arteries." One video promoted a supplement that supposedly fixes hair, nails and joints, but the researchers could not find any trace of the product online.

Medical professionals are concerned. Dr. Emma Runswick of the British Medical Association said that social media platforms "must do more to stop the rise of dangerous fake medical advice." Professor Frankie Swords, the national medical director of NHS England, said that doctors are seeing more patients who are worried and confused by false advice. Meanwhile, in some cases, scammers have used AI to copy the faces and voices of real doctors without their permission.

TikTok disputed the research, pointing out that it was carried out by a marketing agency with commercial interests. The company says it removes harmful health misinformation and works with the World Health Organization and the NHS. Its rules also ban impersonation and misleading AI-generated content. However, an investigation by the fact-checking organization Science Feedback found that although TikTok removes most of this content, some fake accounts reappeared quickly.
Experts advise people to be suspicious of accounts that give confident medical advice while selling supplements or other products, and to check health information with reliable sources.
